Introduction to Professional Skills & Johari Window

Self-Awareness, Character Pillars & Dynamic Interpersonal Growth

Academic Lead:Mrs. Ishara Raviharee Weerasinghe(Senior Lecturer in English | Lecturer In Charge)
SLIIT City Uni • Professional Skills Assessment Standard
Curriculum Overview & Context

Establishes the foundational distinction between technical, soft, and transferable competencies. Explores the internal compass shaping workplace character and introduces the 1955 Johari Window model for expanding interpersonal awareness.

Core Competencies & Learning Objectives

  • →Distinguish between Technical Skills, Soft Skills, and Transferable Meta-Competencies.
  • →Analyze the four connected elements of Character Architecture: Values, Beliefs, Attitudes, and Outcomes.
  • →Apply the Johari Window framework to plot personal strengths across the four quadrants.
  • →Understand how soliciting feedback shrinks the Blind Spot and how candid disclosure shrinks the Façade.
  • →Cultivate a Growth Mindset and an Internal Locus of Control for organizational resilience.

Workplace Skills Taxonomy

The Three Dimensions of Professional Capability

In the modern knowledge economy, career excellence is not determined by coding or technical prowess alone. The curriculum establishes a rigorous tripartite classification of competencies required to thrive in multidisciplinary teams.

While hard technical knowledge gets the candidate an interview, it is soft and transferable competencies that ensure long-term retention, cross-functional respect, and executive promotions.

Technical Skills (Hard Skills):Job-specific, domain-bound competencies such as software programming, system architecture, database design, and algorithmic optimization.
Soft Skills (Interpersonal):People-oriented attributes including emotional intelligence, empathetic listening, constructive feedback delivery, and collaborative teamwork.
Transferable Skills:Versatile meta-skills that transcend specific roles or industries: structured problem-solving, situational adaptability, and disciplined time management.

The Pillars of Character Framework

How Internal Compasses Shape External Reputation

Professional reputation is not merely an outward presentation; it is an organic reflection of four deeply interconnected internal dimensions.

When our core values genuinely align with our daily actions, we establish unshakeable integrity and earn psychological safety within high-stakes project environments.

DimensionCore ComponentsWorkplace Manifestation
ValuesHonesty, Integrity, Responsibility, Fairness, RespectUncompromising adherence to truth in reporting bugs, meeting deadlines, and respecting colleagues.
BeliefsGrowth Mindset, High Self-Efficacy, Internal Locus of ControlViewing difficult technical bugs as learning opportunities rather than personal inadequacies.
AttitudesConstructive Optimism, Intellectual Humility, ToleranceWelcoming peer code reviews with openness, rejecting defensive cognitive reactions.
CharacterRespectfulness, Caring, Moral & Ethical CourageStanding up for architectural quality, supporting struggling peers, and honoring ethical obligations.

The Johari Window Model (Luft & Ingham, 1955)

A Mathematical & Psychological Matrix of Awareness

Conceived by Joseph Luft and Harrington Ingham in 1955, the Johari Window is a cognitive tool for mapping and accelerating interpersonal awareness. It compares what an individual knows about themselves against what others perceive in them.

The overarching objective in professional leadership is to maximize the Open Area (Arena) while intentionally reducing the Blind Area through requested feedback and the Hidden Area through judicious self-disclosure.

1. Open Area (Arena):Known to Self & Known to Others. The zone of transparent collaboration, established mutual trust, and shared clarity. High arena size correlates with superior team velocity.
2. Blind Area (Blind Spot):Unknown to Self & Known to Others. Unconscious habits, vocal ticks, or latent mediation strengths. Can only be identified and shrunk through actively soliciting candid feedback.
3. Hidden Area (Façade):Known to Self & Unknown to Others. Private anxieties, fears of negative appraisal, or hidden talents. Reduced safely through gradual, authentic self-disclosure.
4. Unknown Area:Unknown to Self & Unknown to Others. Dormant potential, undiscovered leadership in corporate crises, and latent capabilities awakened only through novel challenges.

Chapter 01 Experiential Synthesis/Teran Rathnayake (SA25610122)/SLIIT City Uni

Connecting Theory to Practice: Undergraduate & Developer

Reflective analysis connecting Introduction to Professional Skills & Johari Window to coursework at SLIIT City Uni, software engineering projects (LA'CEDRA, TechMart, ApPoint), digital systems at LA'CEDRA, and collaborative teamwork.

01. Meaning & Conceptual Core

This topic defines the foundational architecture of workplace competence by distinguishing between job-specific technical skills, interpersonal soft skills, and cross-functional transferable abilities. Central to this is the Johari Window (Luft & Ingham, 1955), a cognitive psychological model mapping self-awareness across four distinct interpersonal quadrants based on what is known and unknown to oneself and others.

02. Key Theoretical Concepts Acquired
→Tripartite Skills Taxonomy: Hard technical skills open doors, but soft and transferable skills ensure long-term retention and leadership.
→The Pillars of Character Framework: How internal Values, Beliefs, and Attitudes organically produce external workplace Character.
→Johari Window 4 Quadrants: Open Area (Arena), Blind Area (Blind Spot), Hidden Area (Façade), and Unknown Area.
→Dynamic Quadrant Modification: Proactively shrinking Blind Spots through soliciting feedback and reducing Façades through judicious disclosure.
→Mindset Theory (Carol Dweck, 2006): Embracing a Growth Mindset and Internal Locus of Control over fixed defensiveness.
IT//EQ
03. Industry Imperative — Why This Matters in Tech

Modern software engineering is an intrinsically collaborative human discipline. In high-velocity agile sprints, code reviews, and cross-functional architecture meetings, a developer who lacks self-awareness perceives peer critiques as personal attacks. This triggers defensive posturing, siloed work, and hidden bugs. Expanding the Johari Open Arena builds the psychological safety necessary for rapid blameless postmortems and resilient software architectures.

04. Applied Evidence Across My Projects & Studies

2 Documented Applications
Academic (SLIIT City Uni)Evidence 01

Agile Teamwork & Peer Reviews in HDIT Coursework

During collaborative development assignments at SLIIT City Uni, applying Johari principles helped transition code reviews from stressful confrontations into collaborative learning rituals. Soliciting peer feedback revealed hidden oversights in database query structures and UI edge cases.

Entrepreneurship (LA'CEDRA)Evidence 02

Co-Founder Alignment & Transparency at LA'CEDRA

As Co-Founder of LA'CEDRA, establishing transparent communication with partners regarding technical delivery timelines and personal workload capacity prevented misalignment. Shrinking the Hidden Area (Façade) ensured operational trust when scoping client projects.

05. Practical Workplace & Venture Applications

Scenario 1:Software Pull Request & Code Review Checkpoints

Explicitly requesting teammates to audit code for maintainability and readability, intentionally shrinking the Blind Spot rather than defending stylistic preferences.

Scenario 2:Sprint Retrospectives & Client Requirement Discovery

Conducting blameless retrospectives after shipping features, openly sharing technical bottlenecks, and expanding the shared team Open Arena.

06. Personal Learning Reflection & Self-Critique

“Earlier in my programming journey, I occasionally treated critical feedback on my code or architecture as a challenge to my competence. Studying the Johari Window made me realize that defensiveness simply protects an artificial Façade while leaving massive Blind Spots unaddressed. Accepting peer critiques as objective data has dramatically accelerated both my technical craftsmanship and collaborative poise.”

— Teran Rathnayake, Personal Reflection Log

07. Active Learning Frontiers

Honest self-awareness identifying continuous growth areas:

  • Soliciting critical peer feedback earlier in the development lifecycle rather than waiting until final project submission milestones.
  • Communicating private operational blockers more promptly to co-founders and team members to minimize unnecessary hidden stress.

08. Personal Key Takeaways

01.The size of a development team's Open Arena directly correlates with software delivery velocity and psychological safety.
02.Technical prowess qualifies a developer for an interview; self-awareness and feedback receptivity retain the job and build leadership trust.

Core Academic Takeaways

01.

Technical skills open corporate doors; soft and transferable meta-skills secure long-term leadership retention.

02.

Expanding the Johari Open Area requires soliciting constructive criticism to shrink Blind Spots and authentic disclosure to minimize the Façade.

03.

A Growth Mindset (Dweck, 2006) and Internal Locus of Control convert high-pressure workplace failures into catalytic learning milestones.

04.

A resilient professional character is produced only when Values, Beliefs, and Attitudes remain in harmonious alignment.

Academic Literature & Primary Citations (APA 7th)

Dweck, C. S. (2006). Mindset: The New Psychology of Success. Random House.

Seminal work establishing that individuals who embrace challenges, persist through setbacks, and learn from criticism achieve substantially higher intellectual and professional mastery.

Luft, J., & Ingham, H. (1955). The Johari Window: A Graphic Model of Interpersonal Awareness. Western Training Laboratory in Group Development.

The original clinical monograph modeling human interaction, self-disclosure, and interpersonal feedback dynamics.
